I've been farming this land in Quzhou for five decades. At 68, with just two of us in the household, I don't need to maximize every mu for grain — I need reliable cash income and enough grain to feel comfortable. Stevia has been good to me and it's why I dedicate most of my land to it.

My 6 mu breaks down this way: the 2 mu along the east side runs the standard winter wheat into summer maize rotation — that's what my father did, what I've always done, and it keeps grain in the house without much worry. The other 4 mu stays in stevia. That's my income. Stevia buyers come to the village, the contract price is predictable, and I know how to manage it well by now.

For wheat, I'll plant an improved Jimai variety — I've used it for years and it performs well in Quzhou's soil. Four irrigations: at seedling establishment, jointing, heading, and grain fill. The well is reliable so I don't worry about missing a critical stage. I apply fertilizer in two splits — base and topdress at jointing. Two pesticide passes: one for disease at heading, one for aphids if needed.

For summer maize after the wheat harvest, I go no-tillage. At my age, reducing that tillage pass saves my back and saves diesel. I plant a hybrid —郑单958 or similar — and rely on two to three irrigations depending on summer rainfall. Maize basically takes care of itself once it's established if you get the fertilizer right.

Stevia is where I spend my attention. I prep the beds with rotary tillage in early spring, transplant the cuttings from my nursery stock in late April. I harvest three times through the season — late June, August, and early October. I irrigate five times, keeping the soil consistently moist because stevia drops quality fast under drought stress. I use improved high-glycoside varieties. Potassium is important for leaf quality and sweetness, so I don't skimp on it.
